To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the loss of the NOS cofactor tetrahydrobioptern leads to ubiquitylation and subsequent degradation of the enzyme.
depletion of tetrahdrobiopterin by 2,4-DAP stimulates ubiquitylation and proteasomal degradation of neuronal nitric-oxide synthase.
tetrahydrobiopterin depletion enhances ubiquitylation and subsequent degradation of nNOS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ubiquitylation and turnover of neuronal nitric oxidesynthase (nNOS).
the regulation of the activity of neuronal NOS by tetrahydrobiopterin.
the regulation of nNOS activity through its degradation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the loss of tetrahrobiopterin is the endogenous signal for ubiquitylation and subsequent degradation of nNOS.
the loss of tetrahdrobiopterin leads to the destabilization of the nNOS dimer and enhanced ubiquitylation and proteasome degradation of nNOS.
tetrahydrobioptern deficiency leads to ubiquitylation of the enzyme and degradation of the protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent stabilization of nNOS is an endogenous mechanism that protects the enzyme from ubiquitin-dependent degradation.
tetrahydrobiopterin is an important regulator of the stability of nNOS.
the ubiquitylation and proteolytic degradation of nNOS is regulated by the availability of tetrahydropterin.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ubiquitylation and proteasome degradation of NOS may be an important mechanism for regulating the level of NO in the cell.
ubiquitylation of NOS is a dynamic process that can be regulated by tetrahydrobiopterin levels and the dimer stability of NOS.
the loss of tetrapyrroles from NOS may be an important regulatory mechanism for the enzyme.
